name: Astronomy & the Solar System
description: Questions covering: Planets and Moons, Stars and Galaxies, History of Astronomy, Space Missions...

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the most confirmed moons, overtaking Jupiter?
questions.explanation_correct: Saturn has over 140 confirmed moons, placing it first in the Solar System.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jupiter has 95 moons, Uranus has 28, and Neptune has 16.

questions.question: What is the name of Saturn's largest moon, the only one known to have a dense atmosphere and liquid methane lakes?
questions.explanation_correct: Titan is the second-largest moon in the Solar System, with a dense nitrogen atmosphere and a methane-based hydrological cycle.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Enceladus is famous for water geysers, Rhea is a smaller icy moon, and Mimas is known for its crater Herschel resembling the Death Star.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the shortest day, rotating on its axis in less than 10 hours?
questions.explanation_correct: Jupiter rotates faster than any other planet, with its sidereal day lasting just 9 hours and 56 minutes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Saturn takes about 10.7 hours, Neptune about 16 hours, and Earth 24 hours.

questions.question: What is the name of the largest volcano in the Solar System, located on Mars?
questions.explanation_correct: Olympus Mons is a giant shield volcano over 21 kilometers high, making it nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Arsia Mons and Pavonis Mons are smaller Martian volcanoes, while Maat Mons is on Venus.

questions.question: Which Galilean moon of Jupiter is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System?
questions.explanation_correct: Io has hundreds of active volcanoes due to the strong tidal forces of Jupiter and its neighboring moons.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Europa has an ice crust and a subsurface ocean, Ganymede is the largest moon, and Callisto has a heavily cratered surface.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the longest day, lasting about 243 Earth days?
questions.explanation_correct: Venus's rotation on its axis takes longer than its orbit around the Sun (a Venusian year is 225 Earth days).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mercury rotates in 59 days, Mars has a day close to Earth's (24.6 h), and Jupiter rotates very quickly.

questions.question: What is the name of Neptune's largest moon, which moves in a retrograde orbit and was likely captured from the Kuiper Belt?
questions.explanation_correct: Triton is the only large moon in the Solar System with a retrograde orbit and exhibits active cryovolcanism.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nereid has a highly eccentric orbit, Proteus is irregular, and Larissa orbits close to the planet.

questions.question: Which moon of Jupiter is a target for life-searching missions due to a liquid water ocean under its icy crust?
questions.explanation_correct: Europa hides a liquid water ocean beneath its icy shell, containing more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Io is volcanic and dry, Ganymede has ice and rock, and Callisto is geologically inactive.

questions.question: What is the closest star to Earth after the Sun, located about 4.24 light-years away?
questions.explanation_correct: Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf belonging to the Alpha Centauri triple star system, orbiting closest to our Sun.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sirius is the brightest star of the night sky (8.6 light-years), Betelgeuse is a red supergiant, and Vega is over 25 light-years away.

questions.question: What is the name of the closest large spiral galaxy to our Milky Way, with which we will collide in about 4.5 billion years?
questions.explanation_correct: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is about 2.5 million light-years from Earth and is approaching us at 110 km/s.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Triangulum Galaxy (M33) is smaller, the Magellanic Clouds are dwarf galaxies, and Whirlpool is an interacting galaxy.

questions.question: What does a massive star become at the end of its life when it gravitationally collapses to a point of infinite density?
questions.explanation_correct: A black hole has a gravitational field so strong that not even light can escape from beyond its event horizon.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A white dwarf is the remnant of low-mass stars, a neutron star forms from medium-mass stars, and a red giant is an late stage of stellar evolution.

questions.question: What is the name of the dense remnant of a supernova built almost entirely of subatomic particles with no electrical charge?
questions.explanation_correct: Neutron stars are only about 20 kilometers in diameter, but a teaspoon of their matter weighs billions of tons.
questions.explanation_incorrect: White dwarfs consist of degenerate electron matter, black holes have no surface, and magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields.

questions.question: Which star is the brightest in Earth's night sky, located in the constellation Canis Major?
questions.explanation_correct: Sirius, known as the Dog Star, owes its brightness to its proximity and high absolute luminosity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Canopus is the second brightest, Arcturus third, and Vega fifth.

questions.question: Which Polish astronomer published 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' in 1543, proposing the heliocentric system?
questions.explanation_correct: Nicolaus Copernicus presented a mathematical heliocentric model, which launched the Scientific Revolution.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hevelius mapped the Moon in the 17th century, Brahe collected observation data, and Kepler formulated the laws of planetary motion.

questions.question: Which German astronomer formulated three laws describing the motion of planets in elliptical orbits?
questions.explanation_correct: Kepler's laws were based on the highly precise observational data collected by Tycho Brahe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Brahe could not fit a mathematical model, Galileo used the telescope to observe moons, and Herschel discovered Uranus.

questions.question: Who first pointed a telescope at the sky in 1609, discovering craters on the Moon and phases of Venus?
questions.explanation_correct: Galileo Galilei also discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter, which helped disprove the geocentric theory.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Copernicus observed with the naked eye, Bruno proposed an infinite universe, and Newton built the reflecting telescope.

questions.question: Which English physicist and astronomer built the first working reflecting telescope in 1668?
questions.explanation_correct: Newton's telescope used a primary mirror instead of lenses, eliminating the chromatic aberration that plagued refractor designs.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hooke researched microscopes, Huygens discovered Titan, and Halley calculated a comet's orbit.

questions.question: Which astronomer discovered the planet Uranus in 1781 using a telescope he built himself?
questions.explanation_correct: Herschel initially thought Uranus was a comet and wanted to name it after King George III (Georgium Sidus).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Messier cataloged nebulae, Galle observed Neptune, and Olbers formulated the dark sky paradox.

questions.question: What was the first artificial satellite of Earth, launched by the USSR on October 4, 1957?
questions.explanation_correct: Sputnik 1 transmitted a radio signal for 22 days, starting the Space Age and triggering the 'Sputnik crisis' in the US.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vostok 1 carried Gagarin, Explorer 1 was the first US satellite, and Laika traveled in Sputnik 2.

questions.question: Which Soviet cosmonaut became the first human in space, performing an orbital flight on April 12, 1961?
questions.explanation_correct: Gagarin orbited the Earth in 108 minutes on board the Vostok 1 spacecraft.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Titov was the second human in orbit, Leonov performed the first spacewalk, and Komarov died during Soyuz 1 landing.

questions.question: What was the name of the space mission during which Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon in July 1969?
questions.explanation_correct: The Lunar Module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969, achieving President Kennedy's goal.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Apollo 8 only orbited the Moon, Apollo 13 had an explosion on the way, and Gemini 4 was an earlier test program.

questions.question: Which two space probes, launched in 1977, have left the heliosphere and are exploring interstellar space?
questions.explanation_correct: The Voyager probes sent back the first close-up photos of the giant outer planets and carry a Golden Record for extraterrestrials.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pioneer was launched earlier but travels slower, Mariner explored inner planets, and Viking landed on Mars.

questions.question: What is the name of the large space telescope launched in December 2021 that observes in infrared and succeeded Hubble?
questions.explanation_correct: JWST has a gold-coated primary mirror 6.5 meters wide and is positioned at the Lagrange point L2.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kepler searched for exoplanets, Nancy Roman is under construction, and Spitzer is an older infrared telescope.

questions.question: What is the term for the passage of a planet across the Sun's disk as seen from Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: From Earth, we can only observe transits of the two inner planets: Mercury and Venus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An eclipse involves bodies of similar angular size (like the Moon), occultation is when a planet hides a star, and conjunction is a close approach on the sky.

questions.question: How many years does it take for Halley's Comet to reappear in the sky near Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: Halley's Comet is a short-period comet; its last passage was in 1986, and its next return will be in 2061.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other comets have periods of thousands of years, but Halley returns every 75-76 years.

questions.question: What is the name of the boundary around a black hole beyond which the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light?
questions.explanation_correct: Anything crossing the event horizon is inevitably pulled into the singularity at the center of the black hole.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The ergosphere lies outside a rotating black hole, the singularity is the center point, and the Schwarzschild radius defines the horizon's size.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the densest atmosphere, composed mainly of carbon dioxide, causing an extreme greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation_correct: The atmospheric pressure on Venus's surface is 92 times that of Earth, and the temperature exceeds 460°C.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mars has a very thin atmosphere, Mercury has almost none, and Jupiter is a gas giant with no solid surface.

questions.question: What is the name of the largest impact crater on Earth's Moon, located on its far side?
questions.explanation_correct: The South Pole-Aitken Basin is one of the largest impact craters in the Solar System, with a diameter of about 2,500 km.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tycho Crater is famous for its bright rays, Copernicus is on the near side, and Mare Imbrium is a lava-filled basin.

questions.question: Which body in the Solar System was reclassified from a planet to a dwarf planet by the IAU in 2006?
questions.explanation_correct: Pluto lost its planet status because it has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of other Kuiper Belt objects.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ceres was historically classified as an asteroid, and Eris and Makemake were discovered as trans-Neptunian objects.

questions.question: What is the name of the bright, distant object powered by a supermassive black hole, emitting extreme energy from a galactic center?
questions.explanation_correct: Quasars are the most luminous objects in the universe, visible from billions of light-years away.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pulsars are rotating neutron stars, magnetars have extreme magnetic fields, and dwarf novae are binary stars.

questions.question: What is the term for the streak of light that occurs in the atmosphere when a speck of space debris burns up at high speed?
questions.explanation_correct: A meteor is the light phenomenon associated with a meteoroid burning up in the mesosphere.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A meteoroid is the object in space, a meteorite is the remnant that hits the ground, and a fireball is an exceptionally bright meteor.

questions.question: Which meteor shower, associated with Comet Swift-Tuttle, is best observed in the night sky in August?
questions.explanation_correct: The Perseids are a highly regular and spectacular meteor shower, peaking around August 12-13.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Leonids occur in November, Quadrantids in January, and Geminids in December.

questions.question: What is the name of the phenomenon caused by solar wind particles colliding with gases in Earth's atmosphere near the poles?
questions.explanation_correct: Auroras (aurora borealis and australis) occur in the thermosphere as charged particles are guided by Earth's magnetic field.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Zodiacal light is sunlight scattered by dust, noctilucent clouds form in the mesosphere, and ball lightning is a rare electrical storm phenomenon.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the lowest density, less than that of water?
questions.explanation_correct: Saturn's density is only 0.69 g/cm³, meaning it would float on water if a large enough body of water existed.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Uranus's density is 1.27 g/cm³, Jupiter's is 1.33 g/cm³, and Neptune's is 1.64 g/cm³.

questions.question: What is the name of the huge, rotating anticyclone on Jupiter that has raged for at least 300 years?
questions.explanation_correct: The Great Red Spot is larger than Earth, with winds on its edges blowing at speeds exceeding 400 km/h.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Great Dark Spot was on Neptune, Oval BA is a smaller Jovian storm, and 'Eye of Jupiter' is not a scientific term.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has its axis of rotation tilted by nearly 98 degrees, causing it to 'roll' on its side?
questions.explanation_correct: Uranus's extreme axial tilt means its poles are located where other planets have their equators.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Neptune has a tilt of 28 degrees, Saturn 26, and Venus rotates nearly vertically (though retrograde).

questions.question: Which two small, irregular moons of Mars were likely captured from the asteroid belt?
questions.explanation_correct: Phobos (Fear) and Deimos (Panic) orbit very close to Mars and have compositions similar to C-type asteroids.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Charon is Pluto's moon, Titania is Uranus's moon, and Triton orbits Neptune.

questions.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun, characterized by a lack of atmosphere and extreme temperature swings?
questions.explanation_correct: On Mercury, temperatures rise to 430°C by day and fall to -180°C by night due to the lack of an atmosphere.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Venus has a thick atmosphere and uniform temperature, Mars is much colder, and Earth has a moderate climate.

questions.question: What is the name of our galaxy, which is a barred spiral galaxy?
questions.explanation_correct: The Milky Way contains 100 to 400 billion stars, and our Solar System is located in its Orion Arm.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Andromeda is our neighbor, the Large Magellanic Cloud is a satellite galaxy, and Triangulum is in the Local Group.

questions.question: What is the name of the supermassive black hole at the center of our Galaxy?
questions.explanation_correct: Sagittarius A* has a mass of about 4 million Suns, and its event horizon environment was imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2022.
questions.explanation_incorrect: M87* was the first black hole to be imaged (in galaxy M87), Cygnus X-1 is a stellar-mass black hole, and Ton 618 is a massive quasar.

questions.question: What is the name of the stellar remnant stage of a Sun-like star after it ejects its outer layers, leaving a hot carbon core?
questions.explanation_correct: A white dwarf glows only from stored heat and cools down slowly over trillions of years.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Neutron stars form from heavier stars, red dwarfs are main-sequence stars, and brown dwarfs are sub-stellar objects.

questions.question: What is the term for a substellar object with a mass too low to sustain hydrogen fusion, often called a 'failed star'?
questions.explanation_correct: Brown dwarfs have masses between 13 and 80 Jupiter masses and can only fuse deuterium or lithium in their cores.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Red dwarfs fuse hydrogen, white dwarfs are dead stars, and Jovian planets have no nuclear fusion.

questions.question: Which Greco-Egyptian scholar created the geocentry model described in the Almagest, dominant for 1400 years?
questions.explanation_correct: Ptolemy introduced a system of epicycles and deferents to explain planetary motions on the celestial sphere.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aristotle laid the philosophical foundation, Eratosthenes measured the Earth, and Hipparchus cataloged stars.

questions.question: Which American astronomer discovered in 1929 that the universe is expanding by observing the redshift of galaxies?
questions.explanation_correct: Hubble's discovery provided observational proof of the expanding universe, and the expansion rate was named after him.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Einstein created general relativity, Lemaître proposed the primeval atom concept, and Shapley measured the Milky Way.

questions.question: Which Belgian priest and cosmologist first proposed the Big Bang theory, calling it the 'hypothesis of the primeval atom'?
questions.explanation_correct: Lemaître published his calculations in 1927, independently deriving the expansion rate relation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hubble provided observational proof, Hoyle coined the term 'Big Bang' mockingly, and Penzias discovered CMB.

questions.question: Which two American physicists accidentally discovered the Cosmic Microwave Background radiation (CMB) in 1964?
questions.explanation_correct: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson used the Holmdel horn antenna to detect the noise, winning the 1978 Nobel Prize.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alpher and Gamow predicted CMB in 1948, Hubble and Humason studied galaxies, and Dicke and Peebles designed search experiments.

questions.question: Which female astronomer first discovered pulsars in 1967, although the Nobel Prize went to her advisor?
questions.explanation_correct: Jocelyn Bell noticed a repeating radio signal every 1.33 seconds, which was initially designated LGM-1 (Little Green Men).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vera Rubin proved dark matter's existence, Leavitt studied Cepheids, and Cannon classified stellar spectra.

questions.question: Which American astronomer proved the existence of dark matter in the 1970s by studying the rotation curves of spiral galaxies?
questions.explanation_correct: Rubin showed that outer stars in galaxies move as fast as those near the center, requiring an unseen mass.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bell discovered pulsars, Leavitt discovered the period-luminosity relation of Cepheids, and Geller mapped the cosmic web.

questions.question: What was the first spacecraft to fly by Pluto in July 2015?
questions.explanation_correct: New Horizons sent back spectacular images of Pluto, revealing its heart-shaped nitrogen ice plain (Tombaugh Regio).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Voyager 2 flew by Neptune, Dawn studied Ceres and Vesta, and Cassini orbited Saturn.

questions.question: Which European Space Agency mission landed the Philae probe on the surface of Comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2014?
questions.explanation_correct: The Rosetta spacecraft orbited the comet for over two years, studying its gas and dust activity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Giotto studied Halley in 1986, Deep Impact launched an impactor at Tempel 1, and Stardust collected comet dust.

questions.question: Which American probe studied Saturn from 2004 to 2017, releasing the Huygens lander onto Titan?
questions.explanation_correct: The Cassini-Huygens mission was a joint NASA-ESA venture, ending with a plunge into Saturn's atmosphere.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Galileo studied Jupiter in the 90s, Juno orbits Jupiter now, and Pioneer 11 only made a flyby.

questions.question: What is the name of the American rover that landed in Jezero Crater on Mars in 2021 alongside the Ingenuity helicopter?
questions.explanation_correct: Perseverance searches for signs of ancient microbial life and caches Martian soil samples for future retrieval.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Curiosity has studied Gale Crater since 2012, and Opportunity and Spirit were older rovers launched in 2004.

questions.question: Who was the first woman in space, launching on the Vostok 6 spacecraft in June 1963?
questions.explanation_correct: Tereshkova spent almost three days in space, orbiting Earth 48 times.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Savitskaya was the first woman to walk in space (1984), Ride was the first US woman in space (1983), and Jemison was the first African American woman in space (1992).

questions.question: What is the term for the point in the orbit of a body revolving around the Sun where it is closest to the star?
questions.explanation_correct: Earth passes through perihelion in early January, at a distance of about 147 million kilometers from the Sun.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aphelion is the furthest point from the Sun, perigee is the closest point to Earth on a lunar orbit, and apogee is the furthest from Earth.

questions.question: What is the term for the point in the orbit of a body revolving around the Sun where it is furthest from the star?
questions.explanation_correct: Earth passes through aphelion in early July, at a distance of about 152 million kilometers from the Sun.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Perihelion is the closest point to the Sun, apogee is the furthest from Earth, and perigee is the closest to Earth.

questions.question: Which eclipse occurs when the Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow on the Moon?
questions.explanation_correct: A lunar eclipse can only occur at full moon and is visible from the entire night side of the Earth.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A solar eclipse occurs at new moon when the Moon blocks the Sun. A hybrid eclipse is a rare type of solar eclipse.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the strongest winds, reaching speeds of up to 2,100 km/h?
questions.explanation_correct: Despite receiving little solar heat, Neptune's internal heat source generates the fastest winds in the Solar System.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Winds on Saturn reach 1,800 km/h, Jupiter 600 km/h, and Uranus 900 km/h.

questions.question: What is the name of the icy ring of small bodies and comets extending beyond Neptune's orbit, where Pluto resides?
questions.explanation_correct: The Kuiper Belt extends from 30 to 50 AU from the Sun and contains thousands of icy worlds.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Asteroid Belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, the Oort Cloud is a spherical shell on the edges, and the Scattered Disk overlaps the Kuiper Belt.

questions.question: What is the name of the giant, spherical reservoir of icy comets on the very edge of the Solar System, marking the Sun's gravitational limit?
questions.explanation_correct: The Oort Cloud is estimated to extend from 2,000 to 100,000 AU from the Sun and has not been directly observed yet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Kuiper Belt lies closer, the Asteroid Belt consists of rocky asteroids, and the Heliopause is the solar wind boundary.

questions.question: Which body in the Solar System has the most prominent and extensive ring system, first observed by Galileo?
questions.explanation_correct: Saturn's rings are 99% water ice with minor dust, extending thousands of kilometers while being only about 10 meters thick.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune also have rings, but they are very dark and faint.

questions.question: Which moon of Uranus has the most extreme surface topography with canyons up to 20 km deep, looking like a jigsaw puzzle?
questions.explanation_correct: Miranda features Verona Chasma, the tallest known cliff in the Solar System.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ariel has smooth valleys, Umbriel is very dark, and Titania is Uranus's largest moon.

questions.question: Which blue planet was discovered in 1846 through mathematical predictions rather than direct observation?
questions.explanation_correct: Neptune was discovered by Johann Galle after Urbain Le Verrier calculated its position based on Uranus's orbital perturbations.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Uranus was discovered by chance by Herschel's telescope, while Saturn and Jupiter are visible to the naked eye.

questions.question: What is the largest dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, first discovered in 1801?
questions.explanation_correct: Ceres holds about a third of the asteroid belt's total mass and is the only body there spherical due to its own gravity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vesta and Pallas are irregular asteroids, and Hygiea is the fourth-largest asteroid.

questions.question: What is the name of the diagram classifying stars by their absolute magnitude and spectral type?
questions.explanation_correct: The H-R diagram allows astronomers to track stellar evolution stages from the main sequence to giants and white dwarfs.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Hubble diagram relates to galaxy velocity, Feynman to physics particles, and Penrose to spacetime geometry.

questions.question: What is the name of the nuclear fusion process that is the primary energy source in stars of solar mass?
questions.explanation_correct: The proton-proton (p-p) chain fuses hydrogen nuclei directly into helium nuclei.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The CNO cycle dominates in heavier stars, the triple-alpha process fuses helium into carbon, and the r-process creates heavy elements in supernovae.

questions.question: Which nuclear fusion cycle dominates in stars heavier than 1.3 solar masses, using carbon as a catalyst?
questions.explanation_correct: The CNO (carbon-nitrogen-oxygen) cycle is more efficient at the higher core temperatures of massive stars.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The p-p chain dominates in cooler stars, the triple-alpha fuses helium, and neon burning occurs in late stages of supergiants.

questions.question: Which bright red supergiant in Orion shows irregular brightness fluctuations and is nearing the end of its life?
questions.explanation_correct: Betelgeuse will eventually explode as a supernova, making it bright enough to see during the day.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rigel is a blue supergiant, Aldebaran is a red giant in Taurus, and Antares is in Scorpius.

questions.question: Which blue supergiant, the brightest star in Orion, marks the left foot of the hunter?
questions.explanation_correct: Rigel is a multiple star system whose main component emits 120,000 times more light than the Sun.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant, Bellatrix a blue giant (left shoulder), and Saiph the right knee of Orion.

questions.question: Which brightest star in Scorpius is often confused with Mars due to its red color?
questions.explanation_correct: The name Antares comes from Greek, meaning 'rival of Ares' (rival of Mars) due to its similar color and brightness.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aldebaran is in Taurus, Betelgeuse in Orion, and Arcturus in Boötes.

questions.question: What is the closest open cluster of stars to Earth, located in Taurus, known as the Pleiades?
questions.explanation_correct: The Pleiades (M45) are visible to the naked eye as a small dipper of 6-7 bright stars, surrounded by a blue reflection nebula.
questions.explanation_incorrect: M42 is the Orion Nebula, M31 is the Andromeda Galaxy, and M13 is the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules.

questions.question: What is the name of the prominent globular cluster in Hercules, containing hundreds of thousands of old stars?
questions.explanation_correct: In 1974, the Arecibo message was beamed towards M13 to contact potential extraterrestrial civilizations.
questions.explanation_incorrect: M45 is the Pleiades open cluster, M51 is the Whirlpool Galaxy, and M1 is the Crab Nebula.

questions.question: Which emission nebula in Taurus is the remnant of a supernova observed by Chinese astronomers in 1054?
questions.explanation_correct: The Crab Nebula (M1) hides an active pulsar at its center, emitting regular pulses of gamma and X-ray radiation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Orion is a star-forming region, Eagle features the Pillars of Creation, and Dumbbell is a planetary nebula.

questions.question: In which nebula in the constellation Serpens are the famous 'Pillars of Creation' located?
questions.explanation_correct: The Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula (M16) are columns of gas and dust where new stars form.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Carina contains Eta Carinae, Lagoon is a bright nebula, and Trifid is noted for dust lanes.

questions.question: Which Greek astronomer in the 2nd century BCE created the first catalog of stars and discovered axial precession?
questions.explanation_correct: Hipparchus of Nicaea introduced the division of stars into 6 magnitudes, which is still used today.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Eratosthenes measured Earth's size, Aristarchus proposed heliocentrism, and Ptolemy compiled the Almagest.

questions.question: Which Persian astronomer in the 10th century published the 'Book of Fixed Stars' and first described the Andromeda Galaxy?
questions.explanation_correct: Al-Sufi revised and expanded Ptolemy's catalog, providing the stars' traditional Arabic names.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Al-Biruni measured Earth's radius, Ulugh Beg built the Samarkand observatory, and Khayyam reformed the calendar.

questions.question: Which Danish astronomer in the 16th century made highly precise observations without a telescope and lost his nose in a duel?
questions.explanation_correct: Brahe built the Uraniborg observatory, and his data allowed Kepler to discover the laws of planetary motion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kepler was his assistant, Rømer measured the speed of light, and Snell formulated the law of refraction.

questions.question: Which Danish astronomer in 1676 first proved that light moves at a finite speed by studying Jupiter's moons?
questions.explanation_correct: Rømer noticed that the time between Io's eclipses changed depending on the distance between Earth and Jupiter.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Brahe lived earlier, Huygens supported his wave theory, and Cassini initially rejected Rømer's discovery.

questions.question: Which French astronomer published a catalog of 110 deep-sky objects in 1781 so observers wouldn't confuse them with comets?
questions.explanation_correct: Messier's catalog contains the most famous nebulae, clusters, and galaxies designated with 'M' (e.g. M31, M42).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lacaille mapped southern skies, Méchain was Messier's collaborator, and Cassini studied Saturn.

questions.question: Which American astronomer discovered Pluto in 1930 on plates taken at the Lowell Observatory?
questions.explanation_correct: Tombaugh discovered Pluto using a blink comparator, comparing photographic plates from different nights.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lowell postulated Planet X and founded the observatory, Slipher studied galaxy spectra, and Pickering searched with Lowell.

questions.question: Which Soviet space probe sent back the first images of the far side of the Moon in October 1959?
questions.explanation_correct: Luna 3 took 29 photos covering 70% of the far side, allowing the first maps of this region to be drawn.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Luna 1 missed the Moon, Sputnik 3 was a scientific satellite, and Zond 3 photographed the Moon later.

questions.question: What was the name of the Soviet space station launched in 1986, the first multi-modular station?
questions.explanation_correct: The Mir station operated until 2001, serving as a symbol of Soviet and later Russian space efforts.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Salyut 7 was an earlier single-module station, Skylab was US-built, and Almaz was a military station program.

questions.question: What was the name of the first space station launched by the United States in 1973?
questions.explanation_correct: Skylab hosted three crews and burned up in the atmosphere in 1979, with debris landing in Australia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mir was a 1986 Soviet station, Salyut 1 was the world's first station (USSR, 1971), and Spacelab was a shuttle module.

questions.question: Which private space company founded by Elon Musk in 2002 created the reusable Falcon 9 rocket?
questions.explanation_correct: SpaceX revolutionized spaceflight by regularly landing the first stages of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Blue Origin was founded by Jeff Bezos, Virgin Galactic by Richard Branson, and Rocket Lab by Peter Beck.

questions.question: What is the name of the satellite constellation built by SpaceX to provide global low-latency internet?
questions.explanation_correct: Starlink consists of thousands of small satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO).
questions.explanation_incorrect: OneWeb is a British-Indian competitor, Kuiper is a planned Amazon project, and Galileo is the EU's navigation system.

questions.question: What is the term for the apparent backward motion of planets in the sky, caused by orbital speed differences with Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: Retrograde motion makes a planet look like it is drawing a loop, which was difficult to explain in geocentrism.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Precession is the slow movement of Earth's axis, nutation is a small wobble of that axis, and libration is a lunar wobble.

questions.question: What is the term for the slow cone-like rotation of Earth's rotational axis with a period of about 26,000 years?
questions.explanation_correct: Precession is caused by the gravitational forces of the Moon and Sun on Earth's oblate shape.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nutation is a small wobble on top of precession, rotation is the daily spin, and planetary precession is the planetary effect.

questions.question: What is the term for the small, periodic wobbles in Earth's axis with an 18.6-year cycle, superimposed on precession?
questions.explanation_correct: Nutation was discovered by James Bradley in 1748, attributed to the gravitational pull of the Moon's shifting orbit.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Precession has a 26,000-year period, apsidal motion is orbital plane rotation, and libration is a lunar phenomenon.

questions.question: Which icy moon of Saturn is famous for geysers spewing water from a subsurface ocean in its south polar region?
questions.explanation_correct: Enceladus's geysers feed Saturn's E-ring, and organic compounds have been detected in their plumes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mimas has the Herschel crater, Tethys has the Ithaca Chasma canyon, and Dione shows tectonic fracturing.

questions.question: What is the name of the largest impact crater on Mimas, giving it its Death Star appearance?
questions.explanation_correct: The Herschel crater is 130 km wide, representing about a third of Mimas's total diameter.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cassini and Huygens are craters on Mars or the Moon, and Tycho is a prominent lunar crater.

questions.question: Which two-toned moon of Saturn has one hemisphere dark as coal and the other bright as snow?
questions.explanation_correct: Iapetus also features a spectacular equatorial ridge up to 20 km high, running across half the moon.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hyperion is sponge-like and rotates chaotically, Phoebe is a captured asteroid, and Titan has an orange atmosphere.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the highest average density, at 5.51 g/cm³?
questions.explanation_correct: Earth is the densest planet, largely due to its large metallic iron-nickel core.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mercury's density is 5.42 g/cm³, Venus's is 5.24 g/cm³, and Jupiter's is 1.33 g/cm³.

questions.question: What is the term for the range of orbits around a star where liquid water can exist on a planet's surface?
questions.explanation_correct: The habitable zone (or Goldilocks zone) depends on the star's luminosity and the planet's atmospheric greenhouse properties.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The heliosphere is the solar wind domain, the magnetosphere is the magnetic field, and the convective zone is inside a star.

questions.question: What is the largest known Kuiper Belt object after Pluto, named after the Hawaiian goddess of childbirth?
questions.explanation_correct: Haumea has a highly elongated ellipsoidal shape resembling a rugby ball due to its rapid rotation (less than 4 hours).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Eris is heavier than Pluto, Makemake is reddish, and Sedna lies much further out.

questions.question: What is the term for a class of pulsating variable stars whose period-luminosity relation allows them to be used as distance indicators?
questions.explanation_correct: Cepheids are key standard candles. Henrietta Leavitt's discovery of their period-luminosity relation allowed Hubble to measure the distance to Andromeda.
questions.explanation_incorrect: T Tauri are young pre-main-sequence stars, recurrent novae erupt periodically, and RR Lyrae are older stars with shorter periods.

questions.question: What is the term for active galaxies emitting strong radio waves from symmetrical jets powered by central black holes?
questions.explanation_correct: Radio galaxies (like Cygnus A) show synchrotron emission from giant radio lobes extending far beyond the optical galaxy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Seyfert galaxies have very bright optical cores, blazars have jets pointed at Earth, and starburst galaxies have rapid star formation.

questions.question: What is the term for an active galaxy whose relativistic jet is pointed directly towards Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: Blazars exhibit rapid variability across the spectrum due to relativistic beaming in the jet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Quasars emit energy in all directions, radio galaxies have jets seen from the side, and Seyfert galaxies have less luminous active cores.

questions.question: What is the maximum mass limit for a stable white dwarf, equal to about 1.44 solar masses?
questions.explanation_correct: The Chandrasekhar limit is set by electron degeneracy pressure, which cannot balance gravity above 1.44 solar masses.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The TOV limit applies to neutron stars (about 2.17 solar masses), the Roche limit concerns tidal tearing, and the event horizon is a black hole boundary.

questions.question: What is the maximum mass limit for a stable neutron star, beyond which it collapses into a black hole?
questions.explanation_correct: The TOV limit is about 2.17 solar masses, marking the limit of neutron degeneracy pressure.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Chandrasekhar limit applies to white dwarfs, the Roche limit concerns tidal forces, and the Schwarzschild radius defines the black hole size.

questions.question: What is the term for a runaway thermonuclear explosion on a white dwarf's surface in a close binary system?
questions.explanation_correct: A nova explosion does not destroy the white dwarf, allowing the accretion process to repeat.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A supernova destroys the star, a gamma-ray burst is a beam of high energy, and a kilonova is a merger of neutron stars.

questions.question: What is the term for the cataclysmic explosion resulting from the merger of two neutron stars?
questions.explanation_correct: Kilonovae undergo rapid neutron capture (r-process), creating heavy elements like gold and platinum.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A classical nova is surface fusion, a Type Ia supernova is a white dwarf explosion, and a hypernova is a massive star collapse.

questions.question: Which type of supernova results from the complete thermonuclear destruction of a white dwarf exceeding the Chandrasekhar limit?
questions.explanation_correct: Type Ia supernovae have a uniform peak luminosity, allowing them to serve as standard candles to measure cosmic expansion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Types II and Ib are core-collapse events of single massive stars, and a kilonova is a merger event.

questions.question: What is the term for a small, dark nebula of gas and dust from which star formation occurs?
questions.explanation_correct: Bok globules are dense, cold clouds where protostellar systems form.
questions.explanation_incorrect: H II regions are ionized hydrogen, a stellar cocoon surrounds a single star, and dark nebulae is a broader class.

questions.question: Which French physicist demonstrated Earth's rotation in 1851 using a pendulum suspended in the Paris Panthéon?
questions.explanation_correct: Foucault's pendulum shifts its plane of oscillation due to the Coriolis effect caused by Earth's spin.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Biot studied magnetism, Fizeau measured the speed of light on Earth, and Becquerel discovered radioactivity.

questions.question: Which Swiss-American astronomer first postulated dark matter in galaxy clusters in 1933, calling it 'dunkle Materie'?
questions.explanation_correct: Zwicky studied the velocities of galaxies in the Coma Cluster, finding anomalous mass differences.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Oort studied Milky Way rotation and the comet cloud, Hubble studied expansion, and Baade defined stellar populations.

questions.question: Which astronomer proposed the existence of a spherical cloud of comets surrounding the Solar System in 1950?
questions.explanation_correct: Jan Oort proposed the cloud to explain why long-period comets continue to appear despite being destroyed on perihelion passages.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kuiper described the belt beyond Neptune, Whipple proposed the icy conglomerate model, and Öpik predicted the cloud earlier.

questions.question: Which American astronomer formulated the 'dirty snowball' model of comet nuclei in 1950?
questions.explanation_correct: Whipple's model was confirmed by close-up photos of Halley's Comet taken by the Giotto probe in 1986.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Oort studied the outer comet cloud, Kuiper the post-Neptune belt, and Urey cosmic chemistry.

questions.question: Which astronomer formulated the equation in 1961 to estimate the number of active technological civilizations in the Milky Way?
questions.explanation_correct: The Drake Equation estimates factors like star formation rate, planetary systems, and civilization lifespans.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sagan popularized SETI, Fermi formulated the paradox 'Where is everybody?', and Dyson described megastructures.

questions.question: Which physicist posed the question 'Where is everybody?' in 1950, leading to a paradox about the lack of alien contact?
questions.explanation_correct: The Fermi Paradox highlights the contradiction between high estimates of alien life and the complete lack of evidence.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Einstein did not research this, Feynman was a quantum physicist, and Drake formulated the estimation equation.

questions.question: What was the name of the first space station launched into orbit by the USSR in April 1971?
questions.explanation_correct: Salyut 1 launched the Soviet space station program, hosting the tragic Soyuz 11 crew.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Skylab was a 1973 US station, Mir was a 1986 modular station, and Soyuz 11 was the spacecraft.

questions.question: What was the name of the first Soviet space dog launched into orbit on Sputnik 2 in November 1957?
questions.explanation_correct: Laika was the first living creature in orbit, but died after a few hours from capsule overheating.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Belka and Strelka launched in 1960 on Sputnik 5 and returned alive.

questions.question: Which Chinese space probe made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon in January 2019?
questions.explanation_correct: Chang'e 4 landed in Von Kármán Crater, using the Queqiao relay satellite to communicate with Earth.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Chang'e 3 landed on the near side, Yutu 2 was its rover, and Tianwen 1 is a Mars mission.

questions.question: What is the first uncrewed mission of NASA's program that orbited the Moon in November 2022 to test the Orion capsule?
questions.explanation_correct: Artemis I used the SLS rocket and paved the way for human return flights to the Moon.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Apollo 17 was the last Moon landing (1972), Constellation was cancelled, and SLS-1 is the rocket name.

questions.question: Which American probe became the first to orbit the dwarf planet Ceres in March 2015?
questions.explanation_correct: The Dawn spacecraft had previously orbited the asteroid Vesta, making it the first probe to orbit two separate extraterrestrial bodies.
questions.explanation_incorrect: New Horizons studied Pluto, Cassini studied Saturn, and Juno studies Jupiter.

questions.question: What is the term for the bending of light from a distant galaxy by a closer massive object, creating 'Einstein rings'?
questions.explanation_correct: Gravitational lensing acts as a natural cosmic magnifying glass, allowing astronomers to see the oldest structures in the universe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Redshift is the expansion effect, aberration is an optical error, and microlensing is stellar lensing.

questions.question: What is the name for the apparent nodding or rocking of the Moon, allowing observers to see 59% of its surface from Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: Libration results from the tilt of the Moon's orbit and its variable speed as it moves around the Earth.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nutation is a wobble of Earth's axis, precession is the axial cone rotation, and occultation is a stellar eclipse.

questions.question: What is the term for the hiding of a small angular diameter body (like a star) behind a larger angular diameter body (like a planet)?
questions.explanation_correct: Occultations of stars by asteroids allow astronomers to precisely measure the shape and size of those asteroids.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A transit is a smaller body crossing a larger one, an eclipse is a shadow event, and conjunction is a close approach.

questions.question: Which icy moon of Uranus is distinguished by the brightest surface and a dense network of tectonic valleys?
questions.explanation_correct: Ariel exhibits signs of past cryovolcanism and has the youngest surface among Uranus's moons.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Miranda has Verona cliffs, Umbriel is the darkest, and Oberon has a heavily cratered surface.

questions.question: What is the name of the furthest large icy moon of Uranus, discovered by William Herschel in 1787?
questions.explanation_correct: Oberon orbits near the edge of Uranus's magnetosphere and is covered with dark space dust.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Titania orbits closer and is the largest, and Ariel and Umbriel were discovered in the 19th century.

questions.question: Which dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt has a reddish color and is named after the creator deity of Rapa Nui?
questions.explanation_correct: Makemake is the third-largest dwarf planet, covered with frozen methane and ethane.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Eris is greyish, Haumea is elongated, and Sedna lies much further out.

questions.question: Which distant trans-Neptunian object has an orbital period of about 11,400 years, moving in an extremely eccentric orbit?
questions.explanation_correct: Sedna approaches the Sun to 76 AU, and its aphelion lies at a record distance of about 937 AU.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Eris orbits closer (97 AU at aphelion), Gonggong is a smaller dwarf planet, and Orcus is in resonance with Neptune.

questions.question: What is the name of Pluto's largest moon, forming a binary system with it?
questions.explanation_correct: Charon has a diameter half that of Pluto, and the two bodies are tidally locked, facing each other with the same side.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The others are small outer moons discovered by Hubble.

questions.question: What are the most common stars in the universe, characterized by low mass, low temperature, and lifespans of trillions of years?
questions.explanation_correct: Red dwarfs make up about 75% of the stars in our Galaxy, fusing hydrogen so slowly they haven't left the main sequence yet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Brown dwarfs are substellar, yellow dwarfs (like the Sun) live 10 billion years, and white dwarfs are dead remnants.

questions.question: What is the name of a class of old, low-mass pulsating variable stars of Population II, used to measure distances to globular clusters?
questions.explanation_correct: RR Lyrae variables pulse in periods of less than a day and have similar absolute magnitudes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cepheids are young massive stars, Mira variables are long-period red giants, and Delta Scuti pulse irregularly.

questions.question: Which red giant in the constellation Boötes is the fourth-brightest star in the night sky?
questions.explanation_correct: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere, moving rapidly across the sky background.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vega is the brightest in Lyra, Capella is in Auriga, and Procyon is in Canis Minor.

questions.question: Which blue star in Lyra was the first star other than the Sun to be photographed and serves as a baseline zero for magnitude?
questions.explanation_correct: Vega was the zero point of the classic UBV photometric system and belongs to the Summer Triangle.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sirius lies in the southern sky, and Altair and Deneb are the other vertices of the Summer Triangle.

questions.question: Which three bright stars form the Summer Triangle asterism, prominent in the northern hemisphere summer sky?
questions.explanation_correct: The Summer Triangle consists of the brightest stars of Lyra (Vega), Cygnus (Deneb), and Aquila (Altair).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sirius, Procyon, and Betelgeuse form the Winter Triangle, and Rigel and Betelgeuse are in Orion.

questions.question: Which supergiant is the brightest star in Cygnus, forming a vertex of the Summer Triangle?
questions.explanation_correct: Deneb is one of the most distant stars visible to the naked eye (about 2,600 light-years), with extreme absolute luminosity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Altair is in Aquila, Vega is in Lyra, and Albireo is a double star in Cygnus.

questions.question: Which bright star in Aquila, the lowest vertex of the Summer Triangle, is known for its rapid rotation flattening its poles?
questions.explanation_correct: Altair rotates so fast (once every 9 hours) that its equatorial diameter is 20% wider than its polar diameter.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Deneb and Vega rotate much slower, and Fomalhaut is in Piscis Austrinus.

questions.question: What is the term for a supersonic density wave in the interstellar medium caused by a supernova explosion?
questions.explanation_correct: The shock wave compresses gas clouds, which often triggers gravitational collapse and the birth of new stars.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Stellar wind is a continuous stream of particles, a jet is a narrow beam of matter, and synchrotron waves are electromagnetic emissions.

questions.question: What is the optical phenomenon of light refracting in ice crystals of cirrus clouds, creating a ring around the Sun or Moon?
questions.explanation_correct: A 22-degree halo is the most common form, caused by the hexagonal structure of atmospheric ice crystals.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rainbows occur in liquid drops, iridescence is a cloud color effect, and a corona is caused by diffraction in water droplets.

questions.question: What is the rare atmospheric optical phenomenon of mock suns appearing on either side of the Sun?
questions.explanation_correct: Sundogs (parhelia) occur when light refracts through flat, hexagonal ice crystals drifting horizontally in the air.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Light pillars are vertical bands of light, a green flash is seen at sunset, and a mirage is temperature-induced.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the most confirmed moons, overtaking Jupiter?
questions.explanation_correct: Saturn has over 140 confirmed moons, placing it first in the Solar System.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jupiter has 95 moons, Uranus has 28, and Neptune has 16.

questions.question: What is the name of Saturn's largest moon, the only one known to have a dense atmosphere and liquid methane lakes?
questions.explanation_correct: Titan is the second-largest moon in the Solar System, with a dense nitrogen atmosphere and a methane-based hydrological cycle.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Enceladus is famous for water geysers, Rhea is a smaller icy moon, and Mimas is known for its crater Herschel resembling the Death Star.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the shortest day, rotating on its axis in less than 10 hours?
questions.explanation_correct: Jupiter rotates faster than any other planet, with its sidereal day lasting just 9 hours and 56 minutes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Saturn takes about 10.7 hours, Neptune about 16 hours, and Earth 24 hours.

questions.question: What is the name of the largest volcano in the Solar System, located on Mars?
questions.explanation_correct: Olympus Mons is a giant shield volcano over 21 kilometers high, making it nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Arsia Mons and Pavonis Mons are smaller Martian volcanoes, while Maat Mons is on Venus.

questions.question: Which Galilean moon of Jupiter is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System?
questions.explanation_correct: Io has hundreds of active volcanoes due to the strong tidal forces of Jupiter and its neighboring moons.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Europa has an ice crust and a subsurface ocean, Ganymede is the largest moon, and Callisto has a heavily cratered surface.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the longest day, lasting about 243 Earth days?
questions.explanation_correct: Venus's rotation on its axis takes longer than its orbit around the Sun (a Venusian year is 225 Earth days).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mercury rotates in 59 days, Mars has a day close to Earth's (24.6 h), and Jupiter rotates very quickly.

questions.question: What is the name of Neptune's largest moon, which moves in a retrograde orbit and was likely captured from the Kuiper Belt?
questions.explanation_correct: Triton is the only large moon in the Solar System with a retrograde orbit and exhibits active cryovolcanism.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nereid has a highly eccentric orbit, Proteus is irregular, and Larissa orbits close to the planet.

questions.question: Which moon of Jupiter is a target for life-searching missions due to a liquid water ocean under its icy crust?
questions.explanation_correct: Europa hides a liquid water ocean beneath its icy shell, containing more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Io is volcanic and dry, Ganymede has ice and rock, and Callisto is geologically inactive.

questions.question: What is the closest star to Earth after the Sun, located about 4.24 light-years away?
questions.explanation_correct: Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf belonging to the Alpha Centauri triple star system, orbiting closest to our Sun.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sirius is the brightest star of the night sky (8.6 light-years), Betelgeuse is a red supergiant, and Vega is over 25 light-years away.

questions.question: What is the name of the closest large spiral galaxy to our Milky Way, with which we will collide in about 4.5 billion years?
questions.explanation_correct: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is about 2.5 million light-years from Earth and is approaching us at 110 km/s.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Triangulum Galaxy (M33) is smaller, the Magellanic Clouds are dwarf galaxies, and Whirlpool is an interacting galaxy.

questions.question: What does a very massive star become at the end of its life when its core collapses beyond the point where not even light can escape?
questions.explanation_correct: A very massive star can collapse into a black hole when gravity overwhelms all other forces. In that case, an event horizon forms around the collapsed core.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A white dwarf is the remnant of low-mass stars, a neutron star forms from somewhat less massive stars, and a red giant is an earlier stage of stellar evolution.

questions.question: What is the name of the dense remnant of a supernova made mostly of neutrons?
questions.explanation_correct: A neutron star is the collapsed core left after some supernova explosions and is made mostly of neutron-degenerate matter.
questions.explanation_incorrect: White dwarfs are supported by electron degeneracy pressure, black holes have an event horizon, and magnetars are neutron stars with extremely strong magnetic fields.

questions.question: Which star is the brightest in Earth's night sky, located in the constellation Canis Major?
questions.explanation_correct: Sirius, known as the Dog Star, owes its brightness to its proximity and high absolute luminosity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Canopus is the second brightest, Arcturus third, and Vega fifth.

questions.question: Which Polish astronomer published 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' in 1543, proposing the heliocentric system?
questions.explanation_correct: Nicolaus Copernicus presented a mathematical heliocentric model, which launched the Scientific Revolution.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hevelius mapped the Moon in the 17th century, Brahe collected observation data, and Kepler formulated the laws of planetary motion.

questions.question: Which German astronomer formulated three laws describing the motion of planets in elliptical orbits?
questions.explanation_correct: Kepler's laws were based on the highly precise observational data collected by Tycho Brahe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Brahe could not fit a mathematical model, Galileo used the telescope to observe moons, and Herschel discovered Uranus.

questions.question: Who first pointed a telescope at the sky in 1609, discovering craters on the Moon and phases of Venus?
questions.explanation_correct: Galileo Galilei also discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter, which helped disprove the geocentric theory.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Copernicus observed with the naked eye, Bruno proposed an infinite universe, and Newton built the reflecting telescope.

questions.question: Which English physicist and astronomer built the first working reflecting telescope in 1668?
questions.explanation_correct: Newton's telescope used a primary mirror instead of lenses, eliminating the chromatic aberration that plagued refractor designs.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hooke researched microscopes, Huygens discovered Titan, and Halley calculated a comet's orbit.

questions.question: Which astronomer discovered the planet Uranus in 1781 using a telescope he built himself?
questions.explanation_correct: Herschel initially thought Uranus was a comet and wanted to name it after King George III (Georgium Sidus).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Messier cataloged nebulae, Galle observed Neptune, and Olbers formulated the dark sky paradox.

questions.question: What was the first artificial satellite of Earth, launched by the USSR on October 4, 1957?
questions.explanation_correct: Sputnik 1 transmitted a radio signal for 22 days, starting the Space Age and triggering the 'Sputnik crisis' in the US.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vostok 1 carried Gagarin, Explorer 1 was the first US satellite, and Laika traveled in Sputnik 2.

questions.question: Which Soviet cosmonaut became the first human in space, performing an orbital flight on April 12, 1961?
questions.explanation_correct: Gagarin orbited the Earth in 108 minutes on board the Vostok 1 spacecraft.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Titov was the second human in orbit, Leonov performed the first spacewalk, and Komarov died during Soyuz 1 landing.

questions.question: What was the name of the space mission during which Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon in July 1969?
questions.explanation_correct: The Lunar Module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969, achieving President Kennedy's goal.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Apollo 8 only orbited the Moon, Apollo 13 had an explosion on the way, and Gemini 4 was an earlier test program.

questions.question: Which two space probes, launched in 1977, have left the heliosphere and are exploring interstellar space?
questions.explanation_correct: The Voyager probes sent back the first close-up photos of the giant outer planets and carry a Golden Record for extraterrestrials.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pioneer was launched earlier but travels slower, Mariner explored inner planets, and Viking landed on Mars.

questions.question: What is the name of the large space telescope launched in December 2021 that observes in infrared and succeeded Hubble?
questions.explanation_correct: JWST has a gold-coated primary mirror 6.5 meters wide and is positioned at the Lagrange point L2.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kepler searched for exoplanets, Nancy Roman is under construction, and Spitzer is an older infrared telescope.

questions.question: What is the term for the passage of a planet across the Sun's disk as seen from Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: From Earth, we can only observe transits of the two inner planets: Mercury and Venus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An eclipse involves bodies of similar angular size (like the Moon), occultation is when a planet hides a star, and conjunction is a close approach on the sky.

questions.question: How many years does it take for Halley's Comet to reappear in the sky near Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: Halley's Comet is a short-period comet; its last passage was in 1986, and its next return will be in 2061.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other comets have periods of thousands of years, but Halley returns every 75-76 years.

questions.question: What is the name of the boundary around a black hole beyond which the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light?
questions.explanation_correct: The event horizon is the boundary around a black hole where the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light. Once something crosses it, it cannot return to the outside universe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The ergosphere lies outside a rotating black hole, the singularity is the central point, and the Schwarzschild radius is the radius of the event horizon for a non-rotating black hole.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the densest atmosphere, composed mainly of carbon dioxide, causing an extreme greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation_correct: The atmospheric pressure on Venus's surface is 92 times that of Earth, and the temperature exceeds 460°C.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mars has a very thin atmosphere, Mercury has almost none, and Jupiter is a gas giant with no solid surface.

questions.question: What is the name of the largest impact crater on Earth's Moon, located on its far side?
questions.explanation_correct: The South Pole-Aitken Basin is one of the largest impact craters in the Solar System, with a diameter of about 2,500 km.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tycho Crater is famous for its bright rays, Copernicus is on the near side, and Mare Imbrium is a lava-filled basin.

questions.question: Which body in the Solar System was reclassified from a planet to a dwarf planet by the IAU in 2006?
questions.explanation_correct: Pluto lost its planet status because it has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of other Kuiper Belt objects.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ceres was historically classified as an asteroid, and Eris and Makemake were discovered as trans-Neptunian objects.

questions.question: What is the name of the bright, distant object powered by a supermassive black hole, emitting extreme energy from a galactic center?
questions.explanation_correct: Quasars are the most luminous objects in the universe, visible from billions of light-years away.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pulsars are rotating neutron stars, magnetars have extreme magnetic fields, and dwarf novae are binary stars.

questions.question: What is the term for the streak of light that occurs in the atmosphere when a speck of space debris burns up at high speed?
questions.explanation_correct: A meteor is the light phenomenon associated with a meteoroid burning up in the mesosphere.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A meteoroid is the object in space, a meteorite is the remnant that hits the ground, and a fireball is an exceptionally bright meteor.

questions.question: Which meteor shower, associated with Comet Swift-Tuttle, is best observed in the night sky in August?
questions.explanation_correct: The Perseids are a highly regular and spectacular meteor shower, peaking around August 12-13.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Leonids occur in November, Quadrantids in January, and Geminids in December.

questions.question: What is the name of the phenomenon caused by solar wind particles colliding with gases in Earth's atmosphere near the poles?
questions.explanation_correct: Auroras (aurora borealis and australis) occur in the thermosphere as charged particles are guided by Earth's magnetic field.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Zodiacal light is sunlight scattered by dust, noctilucent clouds form in the mesosphere, and ball lightning is a rare electrical storm phenomenon.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the lowest density, less than that of water?
questions.explanation_correct: Saturn's density is only 0.69 g/cm³, meaning it would float on water if a large enough body of water existed.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Uranus's density is 1.27 g/cm³, Jupiter's is 1.33 g/cm³, and Neptune's is 1.64 g/cm³.

questions.question: What is the name of the huge, rotating anticyclone on Jupiter that has raged for at least 300 years?
questions.explanation_correct: The Great Red Spot is larger than Earth, with winds on its edges blowing at speeds exceeding 400 km/h.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Great Dark Spot was on Neptune, Oval BA is a smaller Jovian storm, and 'Eye of Jupiter' is not a scientific term.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has its axis of rotation tilted by nearly 98 degrees, causing it to 'roll' on its side?
questions.explanation_correct: Uranus's extreme axial tilt means its poles are located where other planets have their equators.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Neptune has a tilt of 28 degrees, Saturn 26, and Venus rotates nearly vertically (though retrograde).

questions.question: Which two small, irregular moons of Mars were likely captured from the asteroid belt?
questions.explanation_correct: Phobos (Fear) and Deimos (Panic) orbit very close to Mars and have compositions similar to C-type asteroids.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Charon is Pluto's moon, Titania is Uranus's moon, and Triton orbits Neptune.

questions.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun, characterized by a lack of atmosphere and extreme temperature swings?
questions.explanation_correct: On Mercury, temperatures rise to 430°C by day and fall to -180°C by night due to the lack of an atmosphere.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Venus has a thick atmosphere and uniform temperature, Mars is much colder, and Earth has a moderate climate.

questions.question: What is the name of our galaxy, which is a barred spiral galaxy?
questions.explanation_correct: The Milky Way contains 100 to 400 billion stars, and our Solar System is located in its Orion Arm.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Andromeda is our neighbor, the Large Magellanic Cloud is a satellite galaxy, and Triangulum is in the Local Group.

questions.question: What is the name of the supermassive black hole at the center of our Galaxy?
questions.explanation_correct: Sagittarius A* has a mass of about 4 million Suns, and its event horizon environment was imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2022.
questions.explanation_incorrect: M87* was the first black hole to be imaged (in galaxy M87), Cygnus X-1 is a stellar-mass black hole, and Ton 618 is a massive quasar.

questions.question: What is the name of the stellar remnant stage of a Sun-like star after it ejects its outer layers, leaving a hot carbon core?
questions.explanation_correct: A white dwarf glows only from stored heat and cools down slowly over trillions of years.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Neutron stars form from heavier stars, red dwarfs are main-sequence stars, and brown dwarfs are sub-stellar objects.

questions.question: What is the term for a substellar object with a mass too low to sustain hydrogen fusion, often called a 'failed star'?
questions.explanation_correct: Brown dwarfs have masses between 13 and 80 Jupiter masses and can only fuse deuterium or lithium in their cores.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Red dwarfs fuse hydrogen, white dwarfs are dead stars, and Jovian planets have no nuclear fusion.

questions.question: Which Greco-Egyptian scholar created the geocentric model described in the Almagest, dominant for 1400 years?
questions.explanation_correct: Ptolemy described a geocentric system in the Almagest that influenced astronomy for many centuries. His model used epicycles and deferents to explain planetary motion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aristotle laid the philosophical foundation, Eratosthenes measured Earth's circumference, and Hipparchus cataloged stars.

questions.question: Which American astronomer discovered in 1929 that the universe is expanding by observing the redshift of galaxies?
questions.explanation_correct: Hubble's discovery provided observational proof of the expanding universe, and the expansion rate was named after him.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Einstein created general relativity, Lemaître proposed the primeval atom concept, and Shapley measured the Milky Way.

questions.question: Which Belgian priest and cosmologist first proposed the Big Bang theory, calling it the 'hypothesis of the primeval atom'?
questions.explanation_correct: Lemaître published his calculations in 1927, independently deriving the expansion rate relation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hubble provided observational proof, Hoyle coined the term 'Big Bang' mockingly, and Penzias discovered CMB.

questions.question: Which two American physicists accidentally discovered the Cosmic Microwave Background radiation (CMB) in 1964?
questions.explanation_correct: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson used the Holmdel horn antenna to detect the noise, winning the 1978 Nobel Prize.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alpher and Gamow predicted CMB in 1948, Hubble and Humason studied galaxies, and Dicke and Peebles designed search experiments.

questions.question: Which female astronomer first discovered pulsars in 1967, although the Nobel Prize went to her advisor?
questions.explanation_correct: Jocelyn Bell noticed a repeating radio signal every 1.33 seconds, which was initially designated LGM-1 (Little Green Men).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vera Rubin proved dark matter's existence, Leavitt studied Cepheids, and Cannon classified stellar spectra.

questions.question: Which American astronomer proved the existence of dark matter in the 1970s by studying the rotation curves of spiral galaxies?
questions.explanation_correct: Rubin showed that outer stars in galaxies move as fast as those near the center, requiring an unseen mass.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bell discovered pulsars, Leavitt discovered the period-luminosity relation of Cepheids, and Geller mapped the cosmic web.

questions.question: What was the first spacecraft to fly by Pluto in July 2015?
questions.explanation_correct: New Horizons sent back spectacular images of Pluto, revealing its heart-shaped nitrogen ice plain (Tombaugh Regio).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Voyager 2 flew by Neptune, Dawn studied Ceres and Vesta, and Cassini orbited Saturn.

questions.question: Which European Space Agency mission landed the Philae probe on the surface of Comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2014?
questions.explanation_correct: The Rosetta spacecraft orbited the comet for over two years, studying its gas and dust activity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Giotto studied Halley in 1986, Deep Impact launched an impactor at Tempel 1, and Stardust collected comet dust.

questions.question: Which American probe studied Saturn from 2004 to 2017, releasing the Huygens lander onto Titan?
questions.explanation_correct: The Cassini-Huygens mission was a joint NASA-ESA venture, ending with a plunge into Saturn's atmosphere.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Galileo studied Jupiter in the 90s, Juno orbits Jupiter now, and Pioneer 11 only made a flyby.

questions.question: What is the name of the American rover that landed in Jezero Crater on Mars in 2021 alongside the Ingenuity helicopter?
questions.explanation_correct: Perseverance searches for signs of ancient microbial life and caches Martian soil samples for future retrieval.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Curiosity has studied Gale Crater since 2012, and Opportunity and Spirit were older rovers launched in 2004.

questions.question: Who was the first woman in space, launching on the Vostok 6 spacecraft in June 1963?
questions.explanation_correct: Tereshkova spent almost three days in space, orbiting Earth 48 times.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Savitskaya was the first woman to walk in space (1984), Ride was the first US woman in space (1983), and Jemison was the first African American woman in space (1992).

questions.question: What is the term for the point in the orbit of a body revolving around the Sun where it is closest to the star?
questions.explanation_correct: Earth passes through perihelion in early January, at a distance of about 147 million kilometers from the Sun.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aphelion is the furthest point from the Sun, perigee is the closest point to Earth on a lunar orbit, and apogee is the furthest from Earth.

questions.question: What is the term for the point in the orbit of a body revolving around the Sun where it is furthest from the star?
questions.explanation_correct: Earth passes through aphelion in early July, at a distance of about 152 million kilometers from the Sun.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Perihelion is the closest point to the Sun, apogee is the furthest from Earth, and perigee is the closest to Earth.

questions.question: Which eclipse occurs when the Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow on the Moon?
questions.explanation_correct: A lunar eclipse can only occur at full moon and is visible from the entire night side of the Earth.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A solar eclipse occurs at new moon when the Moon blocks the Sun. A hybrid eclipse is a rare type of solar eclipse.

questions.question: Which planet in the Solar System has the strongest winds, reaching speeds of up to 2,100 km/h?
questions.explanation_correct: Despite receiving little solar heat, Neptune's internal heat source generates the fastest winds in the Solar System.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Winds on Saturn reach 1,800 km/h, Jupiter 600 km/h, and Uranus 900 km/h.

questions.question: What is the name of the icy ring of small bodies and comets extending beyond Neptune's orbit, where Pluto resides?
questions.explanation_correct: The Kuiper Belt extends from 30 to 50 AU from the Sun and contains thousands of icy worlds.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Asteroid Belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, the Oort Cloud is a spherical shell on the edges, and the Scattered Disk overlaps the Kuiper Belt.

questions.question: What is the name of the giant, spherical reservoir of icy comets on the very edge of the Solar System, marking the Sun's gravitational limit?
questions.explanation_correct: The Oort Cloud is estimated to extend from 2,000 to 100,000 AU from the Sun and has not been directly observed yet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Kuiper Belt lies closer, the Asteroid Belt consists of rocky asteroids, and the Heliopause is the solar wind boundary.

questions.question: Which body in the Solar System has the most prominent and extensive ring system, first observed by Galileo?
questions.explanation_correct: Saturn's rings are 99% water ice with minor dust, extending thousands of kilometers while being only about 10 meters thick.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune also have rings, but they are very dark and faint.

questions.question: Which moon of Uranus has the most extreme surface topography with canyons up to 20 km deep, looking like a jigsaw puzzle?
questions.explanation_correct: Miranda features Verona Chasma, the tallest known cliff in the Solar System.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ariel has smooth valleys, Umbriel is very dark, and Titania is Uranus's largest moon.

questions.question: Which blue planet was discovered in 1846 through mathematical predictions rather than direct observation?
questions.explanation_correct: Neptune was discovered by Johann Galle after Urbain Le Verrier calculated its position based on Uranus's orbital perturbations.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Uranus was discovered by chance by Herschel's telescope, while Saturn and Jupiter are visible to the naked eye.

questions.question: What is the largest dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, first discovered in 1801?
questions.explanation_correct: Ceres holds about a third of the asteroid belt's total mass and is the only body there spherical due to its own gravity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vesta and Pallas are irregular asteroids, and Hygiea is the fourth-largest asteroid.

questions.question: Which chart classifies stars according to their absolute magnitude and spectral type?
questions.explanation_correct: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram shows the relationship between stellar absolute magnitude and their spectral type or temperature. It is a fundamental tool in stellar astrophysics.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Hubble diagram relates to galaxy expansion, the Feynman diagram describes particle physics, and the Penrose diagram depicts spacetime geometry.

questions.question: Which nuclear fusion process is the primary source of energy in stars with a mass similar to the Sun?
